hypotheses.title: Auction refund loop can be griefed to block claimAuction and freeze funds
hypotheses.description: claimAuction() iterates over the entire auctionInfoData[_tokenid] array and performs an external call to each losing bidder to refund them. If any bidder is a contract that reverts on receiving ETH (or consumes excessive gas), the entire loop reverts, so the winner can never claim the NFT and the highest bidder's funds remain locked in the contract. Since anyone can participate in the auction, an attacker can place a minimal bid from a reverting contract to permanently block settlement.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a contract whose receive()/fallback() reverts. 2) Attacker calls participateToAuction(_tokenid) with a small bid, adding an entry with status=true. 3) A legitimate high bidder wins. 4) When claimAuction() is called, the loop reaches the attacker's entry, the refund call reverts, and the whole transaction reverts. 5) The NFT is never transferred and the highest bid stays stuck.
hypotheses.impact: Winner cannot claim the NFT; highest bidder's ETH is permanently locked in the auction contract; auction settlement is permanently frozen.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a pull-payment pattern (record refunds and let bidders withdraw) or wrap refund calls in try/catch so a single failing refund cannot block settlement.

hypotheses.title: payArtist rounding leaves dust stranded in minter contract
hypotheses.description: payArtist computes each recipient's share with integer division (`royalties * pct / 100`) and then zeroes out `collectionTotalAmount[_collectionID]` before sending. Because each of the five payouts is floored independently, the sum of the five transfers can be strictly less than `royalties`, and the remainder is never re-credited to any collection balance. The dust accumulates in the contract and is only recoverable via `emergencyWithdraw`, which sends the entire contract balance (including other collections' pending funds) to the admin.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker mints into a collection with a price that produces a `collectionTotalAmount` not divisible by 100 (e.g. 1 wei per token, 3 tokens → 3 wei). 2) Admin calls `payArtist` with percentages that produce non-zero remainders (e.g. 33/33/34). 3) Each `royalties * pct / 100` floors, so 3 wei is split as 0+0+1+0+0 = 1 wei paid, 2 wei stranded. 4) The stranded wei is now mixed with all other collections' balances in the contract's ETH balance.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent loss of dust per collection payout; over many collections the stranded ETH becomes non-trivial and is only recoverable by sweeping the entire contract balance (which also sweeps other collections' unclaimed funds), breaking per-collection accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track a per-collection remainder or compute the last payout as `royalties - sum(previousPayouts)` so the full amount is distributed; alternatively keep the dust in `collectionTotalAmount` for the next payout.

hypotheses.title: returnHighestBidder returns wrong bidder when highest bid is cancelled
hypotheses.description: `returnHighestBidder` tracks `index` only when `bid > highBid && status == true`, but it never updates `highBid` inside the loop (unlike `returnHighestBid`). As a result, `index` ends up pointing to the last bid in the array that is greater than 0 and active, not necessarily the highest. If the actual highest bidder cancels their bid, `returnHighestBid` returns the next-highest amount, but `returnHighestBidder` may return a different (lower) bidder, causing `claimAuction` to transfer the NFT to the wrong address and pay the wrong amount.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker bids low, then a victim bids high. 2) Victim cancels their bid before auction end. 3) `returnHighestBid` returns the attacker's bid, but `returnHighestBidder` may return a different bidder whose bid is lower than the attacker's (depending on array order). 4) `claimAuction` transfers the NFT to the wrong bidder and pays the wrong amount.
hypotheses.impact: NFT transferred to the wrong bidder; incorrect payment amount; potential loss for the legitimate highest bidder.
hypotheses.recommendation: Update `highBid = auctionInfoData[_tokenid][i].bid` inside the loop in `returnHighestBidder`, mirroring `returnHighestBid`.

hypotheses.title: Reentrancy in claimAuction allows draining refunds and re-claiming
hypotheses.description: In claimAuction, the loop iterates over auctionInfoData and for each non-winning active bidder performs a low-level `call{value: bid}` refund BEFORE the bid's `status` is set to false. The `auctionClaim[_tokenid]` flag is set at the start, but the per-bid `status` is never updated inside the loop, so a malicious bidder contract can re-enter claimAuction (or cancelBid) during the refund callback and receive their refund multiple times, or re-enter to trigger additional refunds for other entries.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker places two bids on a token via participateToAuction, one of which is not the highest. 2) After auction ends, attacker (or admin) calls claimAuction. 3) When the loop reaches the attacker's losing bid, the low-level call to the attacker's contract executes. 4) Attacker's receive() re-enters claimAuction (auctionClaim is already true so it reverts) — but instead re-enters cancelBid or simply re-enters via a fresh path; more directly, since `status` is never set to false, the same bid can be refunded again if the loop is re-entered through a different token or if the attacker re-enters via cancelBid before the loop finishes. 5) Attacker drains the contract's ETH balance (which holds all bidders' funds).
hypotheses.impact: Loss of all ETH held by the auction contract; other bidders' refunds become unpayable (insolvency).
hypotheses.recommendation: Set `auctionInfoData[_tokenid][i].status = false` before the refund call, and add a reentrancy guard to claimAuction/cancelBid/cancelAllBids.

hypotheses.title: payArtist ignores failed transfers, silently losing artist/team funds
hypotheses.description: payArtist() zeroes collectionTotalAmount[_collectionID] before making the payout calls, and the low-level call return values (success1..success5) are only emitted in events, never checked. If any recipient (e.g., a contract that reverts, or a blacklisted address) rejects the ETH, the funds remain in the contract but the accounting has already been reset to zero, so the collection balance is permanently lost from the accounting perspective and cannot be re-paid via payArtist.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A collection's primary address (or team address) is a contract that reverts on receive. 2) Admin calls payArtist(). 3) The call to that address fails, but collectionTotalAmount is already 0. 4) The ETH stays in the contract but is no longer attributed to the collection; subsequent payArtist calls revert with "Collection Balance must be grater than 0". 5) Funds are effectively stuck (only recoverable via emergencyWithdraw to admin owner).
hypotheses.impact: Artist/team funds are permanently unpayable through the normal path; accounting is corrupted; funds can only be swept by the admin owner via emergencyWithdraw.
hypotheses.recommendation: Check each call's success and revert (or accumulate failed amounts) before zeroing collectionTotalAmount; or use a pull-payment pattern.

hypotheses.title: Merkle leaf lacks collection ID, enabling cross-collection proof replay
hypotheses.description: The allowlist leaf is computed as keccak256(abi.encodePacked(msg.sender, _maxAllowance, tokData)) with no collection ID, no contract address, and no chain ID. Because the same merkle root scheme is used across all collections, a valid proof for one collection's allowlist is also valid for any other collection that happens to share the same root (or the same leaf structure). An attacker who is on any allowlist can reuse the proof to mint on a different collection's allowlist phase.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a valid allowlist proof for collection A. 2) Attacker calls mint() with _collectionID = B (a different collection whose allowlist phase is active and whose merkle root matches the same leaf). 3) MerkleProof.verifyCalldata passes because the leaf does not bind the collection. 4) Attacker mints on collection B without being on B's allowlist.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized allowlist minting on arbitrary collections; allowlist gating is bypassed, potentially draining supply and denying legitimate minters.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include _collectionID (and address(this) and block.chainid) in the leaf hash, e.g. keccak256(abi.encodePacked(block.chainid, address(this), _collectionID, msg.sender, _maxAllowance, tokData)).

hypotheses.title: Auction refunds ignore failed low-level call return value
hypotheses.description: In claimAuction(), losing bidders are refunded via payable(...).call{value: bid}("") but the boolean success is ignored and the bid status is not cleared. If a bidder is a contract that reverts on receive (or consumes all gas), the refund silently fails while the loop continues, and the bid remains marked status == true. The same bid can then be re-processed on subsequent calls or the funds remain stuck in the contract.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (a contract) places a losing bid that reverts on ETH receipt. 2) Winner calls claimAuction(). 3) The refund call to the attacker fails silently; the bid stays status == true. 4) Attacker's bid remains claimable/refundable in later interactions, or the ETH is permanently locked in the auction contract.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of funds for the auction contract / other bidders; refunds can be permanently stuck or double-processed.
hypotheses.recommendation: Check the success boolean, revert or mark the bid as refunded before the call, and use a pull-payment pattern (withdrawable balances) instead of push refunds.

hypotheses.title: mint() accepts overpayment but only credits msg.value to collectionTotalAmount
hypotheses.description: `mint` requires `msg.value >= getPrice(col) * _numberOfTokens` but then credits the entire `msg.value` to `collectionTotalAmount[col]`. A user who overpays (e.g. sends 2x the required ETH) inflates the collection's accounted balance, and `payArtist` will distribute that inflated amount to artists/team. The excess ETH is effectively a donation to the collection's royalty recipients rather than being refunded to the minter. The same pattern exists in `burnToMint` and `burnOrSwapExternalToMint`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker mints with `msg.value` far above `getPrice(col) * _numberOfTokens`. 2) `collectionTotalAmount[col]` is incremented by the full `msg.value`. 3) When `payArtist` is called, the inflated balance is split among artists/team. 4) The overpaid ETH is not refunded to the minter.
hypotheses.impact: Minters can lose excess ETH with no refund path; collection accounting reflects inflated revenue, and royalty recipients receive more than the intended sale price.
hypotheses.recommendation: Credit only `getPrice(col) * _numberOfTokens` to `collectionTotalAmount` and refund `msg.value - required` to `msg.sender`, or revert on overpayment.

hypotheses.title: auctionDemo.claimAuction refunds losers but can be griefed to lock highest bid
hypotheses.description: `claimAuction` iterates over all bids and refunds every bidder whose `status == true` and who is not the highest bidder. If any refund `call` fails (e.g. a contract bidder that reverts on receive), the entire loop reverts, and `auctionClaim[_tokenid]` is never set. The highest bidder's funds remain in the contract, and the token is never transferred. A malicious bidder can deliberately revert on receive to permanently block `claimAuction`, locking the highest bid and the NFT.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker places a losing bid from a contract that reverts on `receive()`. 2) Auction ends. 3) Anyone calls `claimAuction`; the loop reaches the attacker's bid, the refund `call` reverts, and the whole transaction reverts. 4) `auctionClaim` stays false, the NFT is never transferred, and the highest bidder's ETH is stuck.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent lock of the auctioned NFT and the highest bidder's funds; the auction cannot be settled.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a pull-payment pattern (credit refunds to a mapping and let bidders withdraw) instead of pushing ETH in the loop, or wrap each refund in a try/catch and mark the bid as refunded regardless.

hypotheses.title: burnOrSwapExternalToMint allowlist leaf omits collection and contract binding
hypotheses.description: The allowlist node is keccak256(abi.encodePacked(_tokenId, tokData)) with no collection ID, no contract address, and no chain ID. A proof valid for one external-burn collection's allowlist is therefore valid for any other collection using the same root/leaf scheme. An attacker can reuse a proof obtained for one collection to mint on another.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a valid allowlist proof for external collection X. 2) Attacker calls burnOrSwapExternalToMint() targeting collection Y whose allowlist phase is active and whose merkle root matches the same leaf. 3) Verification passes because the leaf does not bind the collection. 4) Attacker mints on Y without being on Y's allowlist.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized allowlist minting across collections; allowlist gating bypassed.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bind the leaf to block.chainid, address(this), _mintCollectionID, and _erc721Collection, e.g. keccak256(abi.encodePacked(block.chainid, address(this), _mintCollectionID, _erc721Collection, _tokenId, tokData)).

hypotheses.title: cancelBid/cancelAllBids ignore failed refund call result
hypotheses.description: cancelBid() and cancelAllBids() set status = false and then call payable(bidder).call{value: bid}("") without checking success. If the bidder is a contract that reverts on receive, the refund fails silently while the bid is already marked cancelled, so the bidder can never reclaim the funds and the ETH stays locked in the contract.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (contract) bids. 2) Attacker calls cancelBid() from a contract whose receive() reverts. 3) status is set to false, refund call fails silently. 4) Attacker's ETH is permanently stuck in the auction contract with no way to retry.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent loss of bidder funds; ETH locked in the auction contract.
hypotheses.recommendation: Check the success boolean and revert on failure, or use a pull-payment pattern where the bidder withdraws funds themselves.

hypotheses.title: payArtist() uses call without checking success; failures silently lose funds
hypotheses.description: After zeroing collectionTotalAmount[_collectionID], payArtist() performs five low-level `call{value:...}("")` transfers and ignores the returned success boolean except for emitting it. If any recipient rejects ETH (or a contract reverts), the funds remain in the minter contract but the collectionTotalAmount was already set to 0, so the artist/team can never re-claim them through payArtist (require(collectionTotalAmount>0) fails). The stale ETH is only recoverable via emergencyWithdraw, which pays admin.
hypotheses.attackPath: A recipient (e.g., a contract artist address) reverts on receive; the corresponding payout fails silently, ETH stays in the minter, and the accounting entry is erased. Admin emergencyWithdraw sends that ETH to adminsContract.owner().
hypotheses.impact: Permanent inability to re-pay the intended recipients; locked/mis-directed funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: require(success, "payout failed") for each transfer, or revert the whole function on failure.

hypotheses.title: burnToMint mints to ownerOf(_tokenId) but charges msg.value to burner
hypotheses.description: In `NextGenCore.burnToMint`, the new token is minted to `ownerOf(_tokenId)` (the owner of the burned token), while the ETH is paid by `msg.sender` (the burner) in `MinterContract.burnToMint`. If the burner is an approved operator (not the owner), the burner pays the mint price but the resulting NFT goes to the owner. The burner has no way to recover the payment, and `collectionTotalAmount` is credited with the burner's ETH.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (owner) approves an operator (or uses a delegation) to call `burnToMint` on their behalf. 2) Operator calls `MinterContract.burnToMint` paying the mint price. 3) `NextGenCore.burnToMint` mints the new token to the owner (attacker), not the operator. 4) Operator's ETH is consumed; attacker receives the NFT for free.
hypotheses.impact: An approved operator or delegated minter can be tricked into paying for a token that is delivered to the owner, resulting in loss of funds for the payer and free acquisition for the owner.
hypotheses.recommendation: Mint the new token to `msg.sender` (the payer) or require `msg.sender == ownerOf(_tokenId)` in `MinterContract.burnToMint`.

hypotheses.title: mint() accepts msg.value greater than required with no refund
hypotheses.description: mint() only requires msg.value >= getPrice(col) * _numberOfTokens and never refunds the excess. Because getPrice() is time- and supply-dependent (salesOption 2/3), a user who sends a generous msg.value to avoid reverts will have the surplus silently absorbed into collectionTotalAmount and later distributed to artists/team. There is no minimum-out or exact-payment enforcement, so users can lose the difference.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user calls mint() with msg.value above the current price (e.g., to guard against price movement). The excess is added to collectionTotalAmount[col] and paid out via payArtist(); the user receives no refund and no recourse.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of user funds (excess ETH) to the protocol/artists; incorrect accounting of collectionTotalAmount.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require msg.value == getPrice(col) * _numberOfTokens, or refund the excess to msg.sender after minting.

hypotheses.title: participateToAuction allows bids after auction end via missing status check
hypotheses.description: participateToAuction() requires block.timestamp <= minter.getAuctionEndTime(_tokenid) and minter.getAuctionStatus(_tokenid) == true, but getAuctionStatus is never set to false after claimAuction(). Once an auction is claimed, the status remains true, so a new bid can be placed after the auction ended and after the token was already transferred. The new bidder's funds are then stuck because claimAuction() has already set auctionClaim[_tokenid] = true and cannot be called again.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Auction ends and winner calls claimAuction(); token is transferred, auctionClaim = true, but getAuctionStatus remains true. 2) Attacker calls participateToAuction() with a higher bid; the require passes because status is still true and the timestamp check is the only gate. 3) Attacker's ETH is now locked in the contract with no claim path (auctionClaim is true, so claimAuction reverts).
hypotheses.impact: Loss of funds for the late bidder; ETH permanently locked in the auction contract.
hypotheses.recommendation: Set the auction status to false in claimAuction() (or add an explicit ended flag) and require it to be true in participateToAuction().

hypotheses.title: burnOrSwapExternalToMint uses safeTransferFrom before mint, enabling reentrancy
hypotheses.description: The function calls `IERC721(_erc721Collection).safeTransferFrom(ownerOfToken, burnOrSwapAddress[externalCol], _tokenId)` BEFORE calling `gencore.mint(...)`. safeTransferFrom invokes `onERC721Received` on the recipient if it is a contract. If `burnOrSwapAddress[externalCol]` is a malicious contract (or the external collection is malicious), it can re-enter burnOrSwapExternalToMint or other minter functions during the callback, before the mint and before `collectionTotalAmount` is updated. The attacker can also re-enter with the same `_tokenId` if the external collection's transfer logic is non-standard, or re-enter to mint additional tokens while state is inconsistent.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker controls or compromises the external ERC721 collection (or the burnOrSwapAddress set by admin is a contract the attacker can influence). 2) Attacker calls burnOrSwapExternalToMint. 3) During safeTransferFrom, the recipient contract's onERC721Received re-enters burnOrSwapExternalToMint with the same or different parameters. 4) Because `collectionTotalAmount` and circulation supply are not yet updated, the attacker can mint multiple tokens for the same burn, or manipulate the mint index.
hypotheses.impact: Free/duplicate mints, incorrect circulation supply, loss of protocol revenue.
hypotheses.recommendation: Perform the mint before the external transfer, or add a reentrancy guard and update state before external calls.

hypotheses.title: cancelAllBids loop can be griefed by a reverting bidder to block cancellation
hypotheses.description: cancelAllBids() loops over all bids and performs an external call to refund each of the caller's active bids. If any of the caller's bids was placed from a contract that reverts on receiving ETH, the loop reverts and the caller cannot cancel any of their bids. An attacker who controls a reverting contract can place bids and then be unable to cancel them, and more importantly, any user whose bid was placed via such a contract is permanently blocked from cancelling.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a contract with a reverting receive(). 2) Attacker calls participateToAuction() from that contract. 3) Attacker (or the contract owner) calls cancelAllBids(_tokenid). 4) The refund call to the reverting contract reverts, blocking the entire loop. 5) Bids cannot be cancelled before auction end.
hypotheses.impact: Bidders cannot reclaim their ETH before auction end; funds remain locked until claimAuction (which may itself be blocked).
hypotheses.recommendation: Use pull-payment refunds or try/catch around each refund call so one failing recipient cannot block the loop.

hypotheses.title: Refund of lower bids in claimAuction re-checks highestBidder, causing non-winner refunds to top up
hypotheses.description: claimAuction() identifies the highest bidder and highest bid, then loops over all bids. Only the exact (bidder, bid) match gets the token; every other active bid is refunded. Because returnHighestBid returns zero when the top slot was cancelled, cancelled bids with status==false are ignored — but the loop’s else-if condition `status == true` refunds any other active bid including bids from the same winner at a lower amount. The winner who bid twice (an earlier lower bid then a higher bid) receives both the token and a refund of the earlier lower bid, so the seller only receives the higher amount while the winner effectively paid the higher amount minus the lower amount.
hypotheses.attackPath: (1) Attacker bids 1 ETH on token. (2) Attacker bids 2 ETH on same token (passes because 2 > returnHighestBid). (3) After auction end, attacker calls claimAuction(). (4) Highest bid = 2 ETH, highestBidder = attacker. (5) Loop refunds the first bid of 1 ETH to attacker (status==true, not equal to highest). (6) Attacker gets token + 1 ETH refund; seller only receives 2 ETH from attacker but the contract paid out 1 ETH from other bidders' funds. (7) Repeat with many nested increasing self-bids to drain contract balance if enough other bidders' funds exist.
hypotheses.impact: Winner obtains the NFT while receiving back part of their own bid; contract’s ETH reserve depletes and later legitimate losers/refunds may fail or lose funds (insolvency of auction contract).
hypotheses.recommendation: Track and refund only bids that are strictly below the highest bid, or require each bidder to only hold one active bid, or refund by comparing each bidder’s total contribution to the winning amount.

hypotheses.title: mint() takes payment but silently drops excess tokens when supply cap reached
hypotheses.description: The loop in mint() calls gencore.mint(mintIndex, ...) per iteration, but NextGenCore.mint() unconditionally increments collectionCirculationSupply and only mints if circulation <= totalSupply. If reservedMaxTokensIndex was set with a stale/higher max than actual DOS, the outer supply check may pass while the inner check fails per-token. More critically the outer check uses _numberOfTokens but _mintProcessing is invoked per iteration with the same tokData; if the user pays for N tokens and a downstream revert triggers, entire tx reverts (safe). The real inconsistency is that `collectionTotalAmount[col] += msg.value` adds the full msg.value even though msg.value may exceed getPrice*_numberOfTokens — excess ETH is silently credited to the collection, not refunded.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user calls mint() with msg.value = 100 ETH while required is 1 ETH; the entire 100 ETH is added to collectionTotalAmount[col] and paid out via payArtist() as if it were revenue.
hypotheses.impact: Overpayment is captured by the collection/team rather than refunded; loss of user funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Refund `msg.value - getPrice(col)*_numberOfTokens` to msg.sender, or require exact payment.

hypotheses.title: Anyone can call updateUseCaseCounter to expand valid use cases
hypotheses.description: The function `updateUseCaseCounter()` has no access control modifier, allowing any external caller to increment `useCaseCounter`. This counter is used as the upper bound in `registerDelegationAddress` (`require(_useCase > 0 && _useCase <= useCaseCounter)`), so an attacker can expand the set of valid use cases arbitrarily.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker calls `updateUseCaseCounter()` repeatedly to raise `useCaseCounter`. 2. Attacker then registers delegations with use cases that were previously invalid (e.g., use case 1000+). 3. Downstream contracts (e.g., MinterContract) that rely on specific use case semantics (1, 2, 998, 999) may be affected if they ever query these new use cases, or the delegation registry becomes polluted with unexpected use cases.
hypotheses.impact: Delegation registry integrity is compromised; unexpected use cases become valid, potentially enabling delegation-based minting or subdelegation rights in unintended ways.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add an `onlyOwner` or admin modifier to `updateUseCaseCounter()`.

hypotheses.title: getPrice salesOption 2 underflows and reverts on price-decreaserate
hypotheses.description: In salesOption 2 with `rate == 0`, `decreaserate` is computed as `((price - (mintCost/(tDiff+2))) / timePeriod) * elapsedInPeriod`. When `tDiff == 0` (i.e. right at `allowlistStartTime`), `price = mintCost/1 = mintCost` and `mintCost/(tDiff+2) = mintCost/2`, so the subtraction is fine. However, when `timePeriod` is large relative to the price delta, the inner division floors to 0, and then `price - decreaserate` is fine. The real hazard is the branch `if (price - decreaserate > collectionEndMintCost)`: if `decreaserate > price` (possible when `timePeriod` is small and `elapsedInPeriod` is large, e.g. `timePeriod=1`, `elapsed=1`, `price=100`, `mintCost/(tDiff+2)=1`, so `decreaserate = 99*1 = 99`, `price-decreaserate = 1`), the subtraction underflows and the whole `mint` call reverts, blocking minting.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (or any user) waits until a salesOption-2 collection with `rate == 0` and a small `timePeriod` is in a period where `elapsedInPeriod` is close to `timePeriod`. 2) Calls `mint`. 3) `getPrice` computes `decreaserate` larger than `price`, causing `price - decreaserate` to underflow and revert. 4) Minting is DoS'd for that block/period.
hypotheses.impact: Denial of service on minting for affected collections; users cannot mint during certain time windows, and the collection may miss its sale window.
hypotheses.recommendation: Clamp `decreaserate` to `price` before subtracting, or compute `price > decreaserate ? price - decreaserate : 0` and then compare against `collectionEndMintCost`.

hypotheses.title: getPrice() uses live circulation supply, enabling front-run price manipulation
hypotheses.description: For salesOption 3, getPrice() returns collectionMintCost + (collectionMintCost / rate) * gencore.viewCirSupply(_collectionId), reading the current circulation supply at call time. Because mint() checks msg.value >= getPrice(col) * _numberOfTokens and then mints tokens one-by-one (each incrementing circulation supply), the price the user pays is computed against a supply that can be changed by other transactions in the same block. An attacker can sandwich a victim's mint: mint a token first to bump the supply (raising the price the victim must pay), or exploit the fact that the price is evaluated before the loop so a large _numberOfTokens is charged at the pre-loop price while supply increases during the loop.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a pending mint() for a salesOption-3 collection. 2) Attacker front-runs with a 1-token mint, increasing viewCirSupply. 3) Victim's mint() now evaluates getPrice() at the higher supply, forcing overpayment (or reverting if msg.value was exact). 4) Alternatively, attacker mints many tokens in one call: getPrice() is computed once before the loop, so all tokens are charged at the lower pre-loop price even though supply rises during the loop.
hypotheses.impact: Victims overpay or revert; attacker mints at a stale/lower price, causing underpayment and incorrect collectionTotalAmount accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Snapshot the price once and use it consistently, and/or compute price from a supply value that cannot be altered within the same transaction (e.g., pass the expected price and enforce it, or use a commit-reveal / fixed price per period).

hypotheses.title: cancelBid reentrancy allows repeated refund of same bid
hypotheses.description: cancelBid sets `status = false` before the refund call, which is correct, but the refund uses a low-level `call` to the bidder. A malicious bidder contract can re-enter cancelBid for a different index (or cancelAllBids) during the callback. Because cancelAllBids iterates and refunds each active bid, a re-entrant call can cause the same bid to be refunded twice if the status update ordering is bypassed via cross-function reentrancy (e.g., re-entering cancelAllBids while the outer cancelBid has already flipped status but the outer loop in cancelAllBids has not yet processed the same entry).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker places multiple bids. 2) Attacker calls cancelAllBids. 3) During the first refund callback, attacker re-enters cancelAllBids. 4) The inner call iterates the array; entries already flipped to false are skipped, but entries not yet processed by the outer loop are still true and get refunded by the inner call. 5) Outer loop then processes the same entries (now false) and skips them — no double refund here, but the attacker can re-enter cancelBid with a stale index if the outer loop hasn't updated it yet. More critically, the attacker can re-enter participateToAuction to add a new bid and then cancel it, or re-enter cancelBid on an index whose status was just set false but whose refund is still in flight.
hypotheses.impact: Potential double-refund of the same bid, draining contract ETH and making other bidders' refunds unpayable.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a nonReentrant guard to cancelBid, cancelAllBids, and claimAuction.

hypotheses.title: burnToMint reads ownerOf after external burn, enabling reentrancy via _burn
hypotheses.description: burnToMint calls `_mintProcessing(mintIndex, ownerOf(_tokenId), ...)` which performs `_safeMint` (invoking onERC721Received on the recipient) and then `_burn(_tokenId)`. The `_safeMint` callback happens BEFORE `_burn`, so a malicious recipient contract can re-enter burnToMint or other functions while the burn token still exists and circulation supply has already been incremented. The attacker can re-enter to burn the same token again or mint additional tokens.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker owns a token in the burn collection and calls burnToMint via the minter. 2) During _safeMint of the new token, the attacker's onERC721Received re-enters burnToMint with the same _tokenId. 3) The re-entrant call sees the token still owned by the attacker (burn hasn't happened yet) and mints another token. 4) The original call then burns the token, but the attacker has already minted twice.
hypotheses.impact: Duplicate mints for a single burn, incorrect circulation supply, loss of protocol revenue.
hypotheses.recommendation: Burn the token before minting the new one, or add a reentrancy guard.

hypotheses.title: returnHighestBidder returns stale index when no active bid exists
hypotheses.description: returnHighestBidder() iterates bids and updates index only when bid > highBid, but never updates highBid inside the loop. As a result, index ends up pointing at the last bid that was greater than 0, not necessarily the highest, and if all bids are cancelled (status == false) the function reverts with "No Active Bidder". More importantly, the WinnerOrAdminRequired modifier calls returnHighestBidder() on every invocation, so a cancelled/empty auction causes the modifier itself to revert, blocking admin recovery paths.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker places a bid, then cancels it (status = false). 2) Any call to claimAuction() or other WinnerOrAdminRequired functions reverts inside the modifier because returnHighestBidder() reverts. 3) The auction and any remaining funds become unrecoverable through the normal path.
hypotheses.impact: Auction funds and token can become stuck; admin recovery is blocked by the modifier reverting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track highBid inside the loop, and make returnHighestBidder() return address(0) instead of reverting so the modifier can evaluate cleanly.

hypotheses.title: Emergency withdraw drains ETH reserved for pending bids in auction? no; drains Minter balance before payArtist
hypotheses.description: All mint proceeds sit in the MinterContract until payArtist() is called. emergencyWithdraw() sends the entire contract balance to adminsContract.owner(), bypassing collectionTotalAmount accounting. A later payArtist() call for any collection requires `collectionTotalAmount[col] > 0` and then sends ETH from the contract balance, but the balance may have already been moved out. Since collectionTotalAmount is not zeroed by emergencyWithdraw(), artists retain a non-zero claim against an empty contract.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not exploitable by an untrusted external actor directly — emergencyWithdraw is guarded by FunctionAdminRequired — so per rules this is out-of-scope as an attack, but the accounting flaw (balance moved without zeroing per-collection claims) can lead to payArtist reverting and pending artist/team payouts becoming unpayable after any emergency withdrawal.
hypotheses.impact: Pending artist/team royalties can be frozen/permanently unpayable if emergencyWithdraw is used before payArtist, because the per-collection accounting claims survive but the ETH backing them is gone.
hypotheses.recommendation: Zero all collectionTotalAmount entries or require payArtist before allowing emergencyWithdraw; alternatively track a reserve equal to sum(collectionTotalAmount).

hypotheses.title: auctionDemo refund loop uses original bid amount after highest bidder check
hypotheses.description: claimAuction() iterates all bids and for each non-winner entry does `call{value: bid}("")` without checking `success`. If any bidder is a contract that reverts on receive, the refund silently fails while `auctionClaim[_tokenid] = true` was already set, permanently preventing re-claim. Unlike winner payout, the loser's bid stays in the contract — but the loop continues, so no revert protects the loser. Funds remain in auctionDemo but the claim flag blocks any later refund path.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker bids with a contract that reverts on receive, becomes a losing bidder, then another party triggers claimAuction(); attacker's bid is stuck and auctionClaim is set. The attacker can never retrieve their bid, and no other function refunds.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent loss of the losing bidder's ETH; contract accumulates unreachable funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Check `success` and revert, or use a pull-pattern (withdrawable balance) instead of push.

hypotheses.title: mint() updates collectionTotalAmount after external gencore.mint calls
hypotheses.description: In mint(), the loop calls `gencore.mint(...)` for each token, and only AFTER the loop does it update `collectionTotalAmount[col]`. gencore.mint calls `_mintProcessing` which calls `_safeMint`, invoking `onERC721Received` on the recipient if it is a contract. A malicious recipient contract can re-enter mint() during the callback. Because `collectionTotalAmount` is not yet updated and `viewCirSupply` is incremented inside gencore.mint, the attacker can mint additional tokens in the re-entrant call, potentially exceeding intended limits or manipulating the salesOption 3 price calculation (which reads `viewCirSupply`).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a contract that implements onERC721Received and calls back into mint(). 2) Attacker calls mint() with _mintTo = attacker contract. 3) During _safeMint, the callback re-enters mint() with additional parameters. 4) The re-entrant call sees an incremented circulation supply and can mint more tokens, or exploit salesOption 3's price formula which depends on viewCirSupply.
hypotheses.impact: Over-minting, incorrect pricing, potential supply cap bypass.
hypotheses.recommendation: Update collectionTotalAmount and any other state before the mint loop, and add a reentrancy guard.

hypotheses.title: cancelAllBids / cancelBid refunds to bidder (msg.sender) rather than listener
hypotheses.description: cancelBid() sets `status = false` before sending ETH via `call` and does not require success. If the bidder is a contract that reverts on receive, their ETH stays in the contract with status already flipped to false, so cancelBid cannot be retried (require status==true fails) and claimAuction ignores inactive bids. The funds are effectively stranded.
hypotheses.attackPath: A contract bidder calls cancelBid() and reverts on receive inside the same tx path (or self-destructs/blocks), the bid is marked inactive but ETH remains in auctionDemo with no path to recover it.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent loss of the bidder's ETH; contract insolvency in the sense of accounting mismatch between bid status and balance.
hypotheses.recommendation: Only flip `status = false` after a successful transfer, or move to a pull-pattern.

hypotheses.title: auctionDemo.claimAuction refunds losers before/after winner with no reentrancy guard
hypotheses.description: claimAuction() iterates all bids, transfers the NFT to the highest bidder, pays the owner, and refunds every other active bidder via low-level call. There is no reentrancy guard and no check that the contract holds enough ETH to refund all losers. If the owner or a bidder is a contract with a fallback that reenters, or if the highest bid was already partially withdrawn, refunds can fail or be manipulated. Also, the winner's own bid is not marked inactive, so if the same bidder appears multiple times the loop can pay the owner multiple times for the same highest bid.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker places two identical highest bids from the same address (or arranges duplicate entries). 2) On claimAuction, the loop matches both entries (same bidder, same bid, status true) and executes the owner payment twice, draining extra ETH from the contract. 3) Alternatively, a malicious bidder contract reenters claimAuction/cancelBid during the refund call to double-refund.
hypotheses.impact: Drain of auction contract ETH; owner overpaid; losers unable to be refunded (insolvency).
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a reentrancy guard, mark the winning bid as claimed before transfers, and ensure each bid entry is processed at most once (e.g., set status=false before paying).

hypotheses.title: payArtist sends ETH via call before emitting, allowing reentrancy via receive
hypotheses.description: payArtist sets `collectionTotalAmount[_collectionID] = 0` before the calls, which is good, but it then performs five sequential low-level `call{value: ...}` to artist/team addresses. If any recipient is a contract with a malicious receive(), it can re-enter payArtist. Since collectionTotalAmount is already zero, a re-entrant payArtist would revert on the `require(collectionTotalAmount[_collectionID] > 0)` check — so direct re-entry is blocked. However, the recipient can re-enter other functions (e.g., mint, burnToMint) or re-enter payArtist for a different collection that still has a balance, potentially manipulating state or draining other collections' funds.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker is an artist/team address for collection A (or controls one). 2) Attacker calls payArtist for collection A. 3) During the ETH transfer callback, attacker re-enters payArtist for collection B (which has a balance) or re-enters mint/burnToMint to manipulate state. 4) The re-entrant call executes with the outer call's state partially updated.
hypotheses.impact: Cross-collection fund manipulation, potential draining of other collections' balances.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a reentrancy guard to payArtist, or use a pull-payment pattern.

hypotheses.title: mint() loop over _numberOfTokens can be gas-griefed / DoS for large mints
hypotheses.description: mint() loops _numberOfTokens times calling gencore.mint(), and each iteration performs an external call to the randomizer (calculateTokenHash) which may itself make an external call (e.g., VRF/arrng requestRandomWords). With a large _numberOfTokens (bounded only by maxAllowance and supply), the transaction can exceed the block gas limit and revert, making large mints impossible. Since _numberOfTokens is user-controlled and only bounded by viewMaxAllowance, a user can attempt a mint that always reverts, wasting gas, and more importantly the design prevents legitimate large mints.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A collection has a large maxAllowance and supply. 2) A user calls mint() with _numberOfTokens set to a value that passes the allowance/supply checks but causes the loop to exceed the block gas limit. 3) The transaction reverts, and the user cannot mint the intended quantity in one call. 4) Repeated attempts waste gas.
hypotheses.impact: Large mints are impossible; users must split into many transactions; potential gas griefing.
hypotheses.recommendation: Cap _numberOfTokens to a safe maximum, or refactor to batch minting with a bounded loop.

hypotheses.title: sale option 3 mint uses price computed after circulation increment, overcharging same-tx multiple mints
hypotheses.description: For salesOption == 3, getPrice() = collectionMintCost + (collectionMintCost / rate) * viewCirSupply(col). In mint(), the require `msg.value >= getPrice(col) * _numberOfTokens` is evaluated before any mint increment, but `viewCirSupply` reflects current circulation. Since salesOption 3 also enforces `_numberOfTokens == 1` via tDiff check, batch overcharge does not apply, so this is bounded. However, if rate is very small (e.g. 1) and collectionMintCost large, later mints become extremely expensive, effectively locking out future minters and leaving collection supply unauthored — funds/opportunity frozen for later potential artists. This is a parameter-dependent economic flaw.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker cannot directly manipulate because rate is set by admin. However, an attacker can front-run the artist’s first sale with one cheap mint to seed circulation and drive the price to a very high value for subsequent minters. With rate=1 and collectionMintCost=1 ETH, first mint costs 1 ETH, subsequent mint costs 2 ETH, 3 ETH, ... rapidly pricing out real buyers.
hypotheses.impact: An attacker can grief the collection by spiking price early, forcing remaining minters to pay inflated amounts or abandon, reducing total proceeds below expectations and changing distribution. Also, since lastMintDate is set based on circulation, the attacker can chain mints to block other minters for extended periods.
hypotheses.recommendation: For option 3, base price on a separate counter that only increments on successful mints after the price check, or cap the price growth per period; alternatively require that price growth is bounded relative to collectionEndMintCost.

hypotheses.title: mint() accepts overpayment without refund and lastMintDate lag allows cheap back-to-back mints by same actor
hypotheses.description: For salesOption 3, the timing check `tDiff = (block.timestamp - timeOfLastMint) / timePeriod` and `lastMintDate[col] = allowlistStartTime + timePeriod * (viewCirSupply(col) - 1)` generates a lastMintDate that is behind block.timestamp by up to one period. After minting, another mint can be scheduled once one timePeriod elapses from that lag-induced timestamp, occasionally allowing two mints in quick succession when block.timestamp is just past allowlistStartTime + timePeriod * N. Additionally, mint() does not refund `msg.value - getPrice(col) * _numberOfTokens`, so overpaid ETH is silently captured into collectionTotalAmount and later paid out to artists/team, which is not an attacker gain but is a user fund misallocation caused by the contract.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker with first-mover advantage mints once at t = allowlistStartTime + timePeriod + ε, sets lastMintDate = allowlistStartTime + timePeriod*0. Then at t = allowlistStartTime + 2*timePeriod + ε they mint again (legitimate). But between, at t=allowlistStartTime+2*timePeriod-ε the constraint `tDiff >= 1` fails, so they cannot. The lag permits only one more mint per period, so not a genuine double-mint. However, overpayment capture is real: a user sending excess ETH (e.g. from front-end miscalculation or from price changing due to prior mints) loses the excess to artist/team split — an arguable loss to the user rather than an attacker gain, so severity is Medium at most and attacks require the user to overpay.
hypotheses.impact: User overpayment is captured into the reward pool instead of refunded. Combined with option-3 price changes, a sandwiched user may pay substantially more than expected refund; funds are redirected from original payer to artists/team without consent.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute the mint cost, then refund `msg.value - cost` to msg.sender in the same call.

hypotheses.title: setFinalSupply uses mintEndTime without verifying collection actually started
hypotheses.description: setFinalSupply() requires `block.timestamp > getEndTime(_collectionID) + setFinalSupplyTimeAfterMint`. If setCollectionPhases was never called (or publicEndTime is 0), getEndTime() returns 0 and the require passes immediately whenever setFinalSupplyTimeAfterMint==0. An admin (trusted) wouldn't exploit this, but the condition is also exploitable whenever a collection has a small/zero publicEndTime, allowing supply to be frozen before any minting has occurred, permanently capping collectionTotalSupply at 0 while wereDataAdded and setMintingCosts are true.
hypotheses.attackPath: A collection is created with costs set but phases not yet configured; anyone with the setFinalSupply function-admin role (or mis-set role) can freeze supply at 0. This is a state-consistency trap for downstream mint() calls (all reverts "No supply").
hypotheses.impact: Collection permanently unmintable; funds already collected cannot be redeemed by additional mints; user funds from earlier mint() calls remain stranded in the minter.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require both that publicEndTime > 0 and that at least one mint occurred, or that the collection is past its declared end.

hypotheses.title: burnOrSwapExternalToMint trusts arbitrary external ERC721 ownerOf/transferFrom
hypotheses.description: The function calls IERC721(_erc721Collection).ownerOf(_tokenId) and safeTransferFrom on an arbitrary address supplied by the caller (only gated by burnExternalToMintCollections being initialized by an admin). A malicious or non-standard ERC721 can return a spoofed ownerOf (e.g., msg.sender) and a no-op transferFrom, letting the attacker satisfy the ownership/delegation checks without actually owning or transferring any token, then mint a NextGen token for the price of one mint. The price check `msg.value >= getPrice(col) * 1` is the only economic barrier.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a fake ERC721 whose ownerOf returns msg.sender and whose safeTransferFrom does nothing. 2) Admin has previously initialized burnExternalToMintCollections for some external collection hash — but the attacker can choose _erc721Collection and _burnCollectionID to match an initialized hash only if it matches; otherwise the require fails. If any initialized external collection is attacker-controlled or upgradeable, the attacker mints without burning. 3) Attacker calls burnOrSwapExternalToMint, passes checks, and receives a NextGen token without giving up any asset.
hypotheses.impact: Free/underpriced minting of NextGen tokens; bypass of the burn-to-mint economic model; potential supply inflation.
hypotheses.recommendation: Verify the external collection is a trusted, non-upgradeable contract and confirm the token was actually transferred (e.g., check ownerOf after transfer, or use a whitelist of audited collections).

hypotheses.title: airDropTokens nested loop over user-supplied arrays can exceed gas limit
hypotheses.description: airDropTokens() takes user-supplied arrays _recipients, _tokenData, _saltfun_o, _numberOfTokens and performs a nested loop: outer over _recipients.length, inner over _numberOfTokens[y]. There is no bound on the array lengths or on _numberOfTokens values, so a caller (function admin) can pass arrays large enough to exceed the block gas limit, causing the transaction to revert. While the caller is an admin, the function is also reachable via the FunctionAdminRequired modifier which can be granted to arbitrary addresses, and the unbounded loop is a liveness risk for the airdrop path.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) An address with function-admin rights (or the global admin) calls airDropTokens() with very large arrays. 2) The nested loop exceeds the block gas limit. 3) The transaction reverts, and the airdrop cannot be completed in one call. 4) Repeated attempts waste gas and block the airdrop.
hypotheses.impact: Airdrops cannot be completed for large recipient lists; gas griefing; potential lock of airdrop functionality.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bound the array lengths and _numberOfTokens values, or split airdrops into multiple bounded calls.

hypotheses.title: burnOrSwapExternalToMint uses safeTransferFrom which can revert and block minting
hypotheses.category: Denial of Service / Revert on Transfer
hypotheses.description: burnOrSwapExternalToMint() calls IERC721(_erc721Collection).safeTransferFrom(ownerOfToken, burnOrSwapAddress[externalCol], _tokenId). If the external collection's safeTransferFrom reverts (e.g., the burn/swap address is a contract that does not implement onERC721Received, or the external collection has a blacklist/pause), the entire mint reverts. Since the external collection and burn/swap address are set by admins but the token owner is untrusted, a malicious or misconfigured external collection can permanently block the burn-or-swap-to-mint path for that collection.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) An external collection is registered with a burn/swap address that is a contract not implementing onERC721Received. 2) A user calls burnOrSwapExternalToMint(). 3) safeTransferFrom reverts. 4) The mint cannot be completed; the user's ETH is not lost (tx reverts) but the path is blocked.
hypotheses.impact: Burn-or-swap-to-mint is permanently blocked for the affected external collection; users cannot mint via this path.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use transferFrom instead of safeTransferFrom, or validate the burn/swap address implements the receiver interface before registration.

hypotheses.title: burnOrSwapExternalToMint uses keccak(address,uint) but delegation DM hash uses (owner,collection)
hypotheses.description: Delegation lookup falls back to `dmc.retrieveGlobalStatusOfDelegation(ownerOfToken, _erc721Collection, msg.sender, useCase)`. In NFTdelegation.sol, delegators register with the collection address they explicitly specify and use it consistently — but the external collection's "burnCollectionID" is a logical id in this contract (used elsewhere for skip), not the address. If an operator initialized via initializeExternalBurnOrSwap with a burnCollectionID that is not the ERC721 collection address, this fallback never matches any registered delegation, blocking legitimate delegated minting. Conversely, if a delegator registered against `_erc721Collection` for a different use case, the check can allow an unintended minting address.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker registers a delegation from a victim delegator against `_erc721Collection` in DM with useCase=1 (obtained via social engineering or via a different protocol), then calls burnOrSwapExternalToMint using the victim's token and the attacker as msg.sender, satisfying the delegation check.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized burning/transferring of a victim's external NFT to burnOrSwapAddress; the victim's external token is lost.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a stable, well-defined identifier for delegation hash lookups and require explicit per-token ownership/approval rather than only DM status.

hypotheses.title: setTokenHash callable by any address matching randomizerContract slot
hypotheses.description: `setTokenHash` only checks `msg.sender == collectionAdditionalData[_collectionID].randomizerContract`. The randomizer contract is set via `addRandomizer`, which is admin-gated, but the check is on a mutable address. More importantly, if a collection has no randomizer set (address(0)), the check `msg.sender == address(0)` is impossible, so no issue there. However, the real concern is that `addRandomizer` accepts any contract that returns `true` from `isRandomizerContract()`, and the randomizer can be updated by a function admin. An attacker who is a function admin for `addRandomizer` (or who can get a malicious randomizer registered) can set arbitrary token hashes. This is a trust-boundary issue: the randomizer is fully trusted to set token hashes, and there is no validation that the hash is fresh or unique beyond the zero-check.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker obtains function-admin rights for `addRandomizer` (or the collection admin registers a malicious randomizer). 2. Attacker registers a malicious randomizer contract that returns `true` from `isRandomizerContract()`. 3. Attacker calls `setTokenHash` from that contract to set arbitrary hashes for any minted token, manipulating on-chain metadata/randomness.
hypotheses.impact: Manipulation of token randomness/metadata; potential rug-pull of generative art or rarity.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `addRandomizer` to global admins only, and consider validating the randomizer against a whitelist.

hypotheses.title: burnOrSwapExternalToMint mints to ownerOfToken, allowing re-use of external token via flash loan of approval
hypotheses.description: The function transfers the external ERC721 from ownerOfToken to burnOrSwapAddress and then mints the NextGen token to ownerOfToken. A caller who is not the owner must have delegation; but if someone obtains temporary ownership (flash loan of an ERC721 supporting it, or simply being the current owner) they can burn and mint. The minted NextGen token goes to ownerOfToken (the owner at call time), and the external token is permanently sent to burnOrSwapAddress. Because the NextGen token is delivered to the external token owner, any actor that temporarily holds the external token can mint the NextGen token to themselves and then return the external token after the call (if the external collection permits it — many do not — so this is only exploitable with collections whose transferFrom can be reversed within same tx via reentrancy, e.g. malicious external collection set as burn address? But the external collection is chosen by admins via initializeExternalBurnOrSwap, so attacker cannot pick).
hypotheses.attackPath: Requires admin-initialized external collection whose token transfer is reversible in one transaction or whose burnOrSwapAddress returns the token. If such a setup exists, attacker flash-borrows token, calls burnOrSwapExternalToMint, receives NextGen token to themselves, then recovers the external token via a callback (e.g. burnOrSwapAddress is a contract that returns the token). This duplicates the burn-to-mint reward without permanent external-token loss.
hypotheses.impact: Reward (free mint via burn-to-mint) can be claimed without actually burning/swapping the external token permanently; deflates burn-to-mint scarcity and steals value from the collection.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require the minted token to be sent to msg.sender rather than ownerOfToken, or verify ownership at end of transaction / after the safeTransferFrom that the recipient actually retained the burn.

hypotheses.title: burnToMint sends new token to ownerOf(burnedToken), letting borrowers keep minted token from flash-borrowed token
hypotheses.description: burnToMint() checks `_isApprovedOrOwner(burner, _tokenId)` and then calls `_mintProcessing(mintIndex, ownerOf(_tokenId), ...)` — i.e. the newly minted token is delivered to the current owner of the burned token, not to `burner`. If `burner` is merely approved (not owner), the mint goes to the owner who did not pay. But the real economic exploit is: any actor who is temporarily the owner (via flash-borrowed NFT or via a collection whose burn hook returns ownership) can burn-to-mint and receive a new token, then regain the burned token via the external flow. Within the NextGen contract alone, the attacker’s economics require them to actually own the token they burn, so this is not by itself a free-mint. However, combined with any external helper that lends ownership within one transaction (common via ERC721 `setApprovalForAll` revert patterns is not enough; requires a contract that transfers the token, allows burnToMint, and then reverts), it is exploitable.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker deploys/uses a flash-NFT lender that: (1) transfers the burnable token to attacker, (2) attacker calls burnToMint which burns the token and mints a new NextGen token to the attacker (current owner at that moment is attacker), (3) lender’s callback returns the original token via a separate mechanism (e.g. it is re-minted or the attacker’s original approval restores ownership is impossible — burn destroys it, so this is only possible if the “burned” token is re-issued). Because NextGen burn is irreversible, this path is not exploitable without a mint hook, so this finding is limited.
hypotheses.impact: If combined with any mechanism that can restore the burned token, attacker gets a free NextGen token per burn-to-mint cycle, diluting the collection and stealing value from the protocol/other holders.
hypotheses.recommendation: Deliver the minted token to msg.sender (burner) rather than ownerOf(_tokenId), and validate that the burner actually owns the burned token.
